message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it must be returned within 30 days after you move out, unless you give written notice of intent to stay.
• The deposit can only be used for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear, or cleaning if the lease specifies it. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Take photos or video of the unit when you move in and out. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a habitable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, structural safety).
• Landlords must repair major problems within a reasonable time after notice. | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent or pay for repairs and deduct from rent (but do so carefully and document everything). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlords must give at least 24 hours written notice before entering, except in emergencies.
• Entry is allowed for inspections, repairs, or showing the unit to prospective tenants/buyers. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Privacy** | • You have the right to quiet enjoyment of the premises.
• Landlords cannot harass or threaten you. | • If you feel harassed, document incidents and consider contacting local law enforcement or a tenant‑rights group. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice of non‑renewal at least 30 days before the lease ends. | • Provide written notice and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a 3‑day notice for non‑payment of rent, a 3‑day notice for lease violations, or a 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month termination.
• After the notice period, the landlord files a lawsuit; you have a chance to defend yourself. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you receive an eviction notice, consider contacting a tenant‑rights lawyer or legal aid. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • Texas law allows tenants to pay for necessary repairs and deduct the cost from rent if the landlord fails to act, but only if the repair is essential and the landlord has been notified. | • Keep receipts and document the repair. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas does not have statewide rent control; rent increases are governed by the lease agreement. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting** | • Subletting is allowed only if the lease permits it or the landlord consents. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Attorney General’s Office – Consumer Protection Division.
• Texas Tenants’ Rights – local nonprofits (e.g., Texas Tenants’ Rights Coalition).
• Legal Aid of North Texas, Lone Star Legal Aid, etc. | • Use these resources for guidance, mediation, or legal representation. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – look for clauses on rent, security deposit, maintenance responsibilities, entry notice, and termination. 2. **Ask about habitability** – confirm that the landlord will handle major repairs. 3. **Document the unit’s condition** – take photos/video and keep a copy of the move‑in inspection. 4. **Verify utility responsibilities** – know who pays what. 5. **Check for discrimination** – ensure the landlord is not violating fair‑housing laws. --- #### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | First Step | Next Step | |-------|------------|-----------| | Landlord refuses to make repairs | Write a formal notice (email/text) and keep a copy | If no response in 7–10 days, consider withholding rent or filing a repair‑and‑deduct claim | | Unreasonable late fee | Review lease clause; if it’s excessive, negotiate or refuse to pay | If dispute escalates, seek mediation or legal advice | | Eviction notice | Respond within the notice period; file a defense in court | If you’re evicted, contact a tenant‑rights organization for assistance | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, privacy, and protection against discrimination. Landlords must follow strict notice and repair procedures, and you have recourse if they fail to comply. If you encounter problems, document everything, communicate in writing, and seek help from local tenant‑rights groups or legal professionals.
